chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, who said, 'Al-Nadr ibn Qirwash Al-Jammal informed us, saying,'

'I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about camels that have scabies: should I keep them apart from my camels, fearing that their scabies might infect mine? And the animal, I would sometimes let it drink water until it was full.'

So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'A Bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I find sheep, cows, and camels sold at a low price, and they have scabies. I dislike buying them, fearing that their scabies might infect my camels and my sheep."'
So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him: "O Bedouin! So who infected the first one?"

Then the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'There is no 'Adwa (infection), nor 'Tiyyarah (good omen/bird divination), nor Hamah (bird omen), nor Shu'm (bad luck), nor Safra (drinking until full), nor Rada'ah (breastfeeding after weaning), nor Ta'rub (becoming Bedouin after Hijra), nor Samt (fasting of silence) from day to night, nor Talaq (divorce) before Nikah (marriage contract), nor 'Itq (emancipation) before Milking (ownership), nor Yutm (orphanhood) after Idrak (adulthood).'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on keeping sick animals away from healthy ones in Islam?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Kafi records Imam al-Sadiq (as) clarifying the concept of 'Adwa (infection) by referencing the Prophet’s response to a Bedouin, establishing that while disease transmission is a natural reality, it is not a supernatural curse independent of God’s will. The text systematically negates pre-Islamic superstitions such as 'Safra' (watching for a specific time to drink) and 'Hamah' (omen bird), aligning with the Shia theological principle of rejecting 'Jahiliyyah' beliefs while accepting empirical observation. This hadith serves as a foundational legal text for distinguishing between natural causality and divine decree in matters of animal husbandry and health.

en.hubeali: H 14682 – Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad Bin Isa, from Al-Hassan Bin Mahboub, who said, ‘we have been informed by Al-Nazar bin Qarwaash Al-Jammaal who said:

I asked Abu Abdullahasws about the camels who have scabies whether I should keep my camel away from these fearing it might get infected by the scabies, and the animals might have got it until it drank the water’.

So Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> said that: ‘A Bedouin came up to the Rasool Allah<sup>s</sup><sup>aww</sup>. He said, ‘O Rasool Allah<sup>saww</sup>, I come across injured sheep, cows, and the camels sold at a cheap price, but they have scabies. I dislike buying these fearing that they may infect my camels and my sheep with that scabies’.
So the Rasool Allah<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘O Bedouin! So who infected the first (infected) one?’

Then the Rasool Allah<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘There is neither infection, nor bad omen, nor ghost, nor bad luck, nor ‘Safra’, nor breastfeeding after weaning, nor being a Bedouin after Migration (Hijra), nor Fasting of silence for a day to the night, nor divorce before the marriage, nor emancipation before slavery, nor being an orphan after achieving adulthood’.
